```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(AKCatchments)
options(AKCatchments.cache = file.path(tempdir(), "ak_vignette_cache"))
```

Annual maximum summer NDVI (NDVImax) for each catchment from Landsat 5, 7,
8 and 9 Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance (30 m, 1984 on), read from
the Microsoft Planetary Computer, and its long-term mean and trend. The
methods follow Berner et al. (2020) and the 'LandsatTS' R package (Berner
et al. 2023): pixel screening, cross-sensor calibration and a
phenology-adjusted annual peak.

Input, as for every layer: catchments (sf polygons with `site_code`, one
row per catchment, any CRS; a single `ak_delineate()` result, a list of
them, `ak_catchments()` output or your own polygons). Chunks that download
data are not run when this vignette is built; chunks that only compute
are. The other layers are listed in `vignette("delineation")`, section 7.

## 1. Getting the data

Automatic, no login: a STAC search per group of nearby catchments and
year, an anonymous access token, and reads of four bands (red, NIR,
QA_PIXEL, QA_RADSAT) at sample points in each summer scene. Readings are
cached per catchment in `landsat_c2/`; later calls read only new scenes. A
first run for a region over 40 years can take hours; failed scenes are in
`attr(, "failed")`. A progress bar counts the groups of catchments; with
mirai daemons running, groups are read in parallel (`?ak_parallel`).

## 2. Using it

```{r use, eval = FALSE}
x <- ak_catchments(pts)
g <- ak_peak_ndvi(x, years = 1984:2024)               # table of annual values; call on ALL catchments together
attr(g, "xcal")                                      # calibration of each sensor to Landsat 7
s <- peak_ndvi_summary(g, years = 2000:2024, trend_years = 1985:2024)   # one row per site
x <- catchment_join(x, s)                            # onto the catchments, with provenance

d <- ak_delineate(lat = 63.7255, lon = -148.9670, site_code = "SITE-001")
ak_peak_ndvi(d, years = 2013:2020)                   # works, but one small catchment is too few to calibrate
```

The calibration is pooled over the catchments in one call: with too few
sample points that both sensors saw (under 30), a sensor stays
uncalibrated and the values carry the `uncalibrated` flag.

## 3. What you get

`ak_peak_ndvi()`, a table with one row per site and year: `ndvi_max`,
`ndvi_max_se`, `ndvi_max_lo95`, `ndvi_max_hi95`, `ndvi_max_cal_se`,
`n_points`, `n_points_valid`, `veg_frac`, `obs_per_point`, `sensors`,
`share_L5`, `share_L8`, `flag` (`few_points`, `low_coverage`,
`sparse_vegetation`, `few_obs`, `record_edge`, `uncalibrated`).
Attributes `points` (per point and year), `xcal`, `failed`.

`peak_ndvi_summary()`: `ndvimax_mean` and `ndvimax_trend_decade`, each
with `_se`, `_lo95`, `_hi95`, `_flag`, plus `ndvimax_n_years`,
`ndvimax_veg_frac`.

## 4. Uncertainty: how it is computed

**Method.** Annual maximum summer NDVI at 30 m from Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9
Collection 2 surface reflectance, read at regularly spaced points in each
catchment, screened, cross-calibrated to Landsat 7 and phenology-adjusted
after Berner et al. (2020) and the 'LandsatTS' package (Berner et al.
2023). The steps that matter for uncertainty:

1. *Sensors differ.* Uncalibrated, Landsat 5 and Landsat 8 NDVI differ
   from Landsat 7 by a few hundredths, the size of decades of greening.
   Each sensor is mapped onto Landsat 7 with a polynomial fitted to paired
   observations at points and years both sensors saw.
2. *Few clear days.* A year's peak is estimated from the clear
   observations that year, each moved up to the peak of a 7-year seasonal
   curve, so the peak isn't missed just because no clear day fell on it.
3. *Bare ground.* Points that are never green (NDVI < 0.15: rock, ice,
   water) are left out; `veg_frac` is the vegetated share, and the value
   describes the vegetated part only.

**Annual SE.** `ndvi_max_se` = √(sampling² + peak² + calibration²):
sampling is the SD of the point values / √points; peak is the RMS of the
points' peak SEs, taken as fully shared among points (they see the same
scenes on the same days), which is conservative; calibration is the SE of
the calibration curve plus the bias left on held-out points, at least
0.002 (below). Calibration and peak errors are systematic within a year
and do not shrink with more points.

**Two refinements of the published method**, found when testing against
synthetic data with known sensor offsets:

- LandsatTS pairs the sensors by medians within ±7 days of a focal day.
  When the two sensors see different days of the season (they do: their
  orbits are offset by 8 days), those medians compare different stages of
  green-up or senescence. Here the focal day is the one nearest the
  point's seasonal peak, and each observation is first moved to the focal
  day along a quadratic fitted to that sensor's own observations at that
  point. In simulation this cut the calibration's residual bias from about
  0.02-0.03 to 0.001-0.002 NDVI.
- The held-out check cannot see the pairing's own error, so the
  calibration SE has a floor (`cal_floor = 0.002`, the residual bias in
  those simulations). It is an internal figure, not a published one.

**Trend SE.** `ndvimax_trend_decade_se` combines the OLS SE (years
discounted for lag-1 autocorrelation) with the effect of a calibration
offset on the slope: a leftover offset in one sensor becomes a step
wherever that sensor's share of the observations changes (Landsat 5 ends
in 2011, Landsat 8 starts in 2013). The step term is
offset SE × slope of that sensor's share on time. Without calibration,
`sensor_change` flags any trend spanning sensors.

**Not included.** Atmospheric-correction error beyond what calibration
absorbs; low bias of the peak in years with very few clear days (flag
`few_obs`); differences between NDVImax and the vegetation properties you
care about (shrub cover, biomass).

**Alternatives.** MODIS MOD13Q1 (250 m, 2000 on, one sensor family) would
be an independent check on interannual variation; the ABoVE Landsat
products (Ju and Masek 2016, trends 1984-2012; Melaas et al. 2019, peak
greenness 1984-2014) end before most CAKN samples.

## 5. Checking and validating it

- **Calibration.** Read `attr(g, "xcal")`: `uncal_bias` is the sensor
  offset before calibration (a few hundredths is normal), `xcal_bias` what
  remains on held-out points (should be near 0), `cal_sd` what goes into
  the SEs.
- **Sensor steps.** Plot each site's series with the sensor shares: a step
  at 2012-2013 that the calibration didn't remove shows as a jump when
  `share_L8` rises.
- **Published trends.** Ju and Masek's Landsat NDVI trends (1984-2012) are
  an independent estimate for the overlap years:

```{r ju-masek, eval = FALSE}
tr <- terra::rast("ABoVE_NDVI_trend_tile.tif")         # downloaded from ORNL DAAC (Earthdata login)
catchment_mean(x, tr, "jm_trend")                     # compare with peak_ndvi_summary(g, trend_years = 1984:2012)
```

- **Vegetated share.** `veg_frac` should match the non-barren, non-ice,
  non-water share from NLCD (`vignette("landcover-nlcd")`).

## 6. Pitfalls

- Values describe the vegetated points only (NDVI ≥ 0.15).
- Calibrate across all catchments in one call.
- Few clear days (`few_obs`) bias the peak low.
- NDVImax is greenness, not alder or biomass.

## References

- Berner, L. T. et al. (2020). Summer warming explains widespread but not uniform greening in the Arctic tundra biome. Nature Communications 11, 4621.
- Berner, L. T., Assmann, J. J., Normand, S. and Goetz, S. J. (2023). 'LandsatTS': an R package to facilitate retrieval, cleaning, cross-calibration, and phenological modeling of Landsat time series data. Ecography 2023, e06768.
- Ju, J. and Masek, J. G. (2016). The vegetation greenness trend in Canada and US Alaska from 1984-2012 Landsat data. Remote Sensing of Environment 176. Data: doi:10.3334/ORNLDAAC/1576.
- USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 (doi:10.5066/P9IAXOVV, doi:10.5066/P9C7I13B, doi:10.5066/P9OGBGM6).
